Formulation
- Predisposing factors:
  - Family history of cerebrovascular disease (father required carotid surgery)
- Precipitating factors:
  - New onset intermittent neurological symptoms (paresthesia of right hand, transient weakness in right arm and intermittent gait change) evolving over ~1–2 months with increasing frequency
- Perpetuating factors:
  - Self-medication with aspirin without GP guidance; ongoing uncertainty and health-related worry
- Protective factors:
  - Supportive partner, recent normal vascular screening (BP, cholesterol, diabetes), prompt access to GP services
- Summary:
  - A medically trained 32-year-old male developed progressive intermittent neurological episodes (right hand paresthesia, transient right-sided weakness, transient gait alteration) over 1–2 months. Family history of carotid disease raises concern for TIA; urgent specialist assessment is appropriate. No mental health diagnosis documented; symptoms include fatigue and reduced motivation associated with episodes.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Suspected transient ischemic attack (TIA) / mini-stroke
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Obtain urgent specialist assessment to determine cause of transient neurological symptoms and receive appropriate management
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Exclude TIA/stroke via urgent TIA clinic assessment including carotid ultrasound and appropriate brain imaging; provide clear safety instructions if symptoms recur or persist
- Actions (Patient):
  - Attend TIA clinic appointment when contacted
  - Contact the hospital PALS/TIA clinic number (to be provided in notes) to confirm booking if not contacted within expected timeframe
  - Present to A&E immediately if symptoms return and are prolonged/persistent or if new/worsening neurological deficits occur
  - Contact GP if delays in arranging specialist assessment or if further advice required
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Referral to TIA clinic made (urgent referral; expected contact within 1–2 days)
  - Document and provide TIA clinic / PALS contact details in consultation notes for patient to chase appointment
  - Advise patient to attend A&E for prolonged or persistent neurological symptoms (to exclude stroke)
  - Offer telephone assessment/support if symptoms recur prior to specialist review

Secondary Problem: Intermittent fatigue, nausea, reduced motivation/energy
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Improve energy levels and reduce nausea once serious neurological causes are excluded
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Reassess these symptoms after specialist evaluation and investigations; consider further assessment/treatment if symptoms persist
- Actions (Patient):
  - Report fatigue and nausea to TIA clinic/GP during assessments and follow-up
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Reassess physical and mental health following TIA clinic outcomes; initiate further investigations or referrals as indicated (not yet documented in this consultation)

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered:
  - Nature of suspected diagnosis (TIA/mini-stroke) and urgency of assessment
  - What the TIA clinic will likely assess (carotid ultrasound, possible brain scan)
  - Advice to attend A&E urgently if symptoms recur and persist/prolong (possible stroke)
  - Instruction to contact hospital PALS/TIA clinic to confirm appointment; GP to leave contact number in notes
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening:
  - Prolonged or persistent neurological symptoms (weakness, numbness)
  - New or worsening difficulty with swallowing, speech, vision, or sustained inability to perform tasks (e.g., difficulty holding a cup)
- Coping Strategies:
  - Not recorded (advice focused on urgent medical assessment and safety planning)
